extracted.intended_audience: foreign attorneys seeking USPTO registration (foreign trademark practitioners), USPTO/OED staff, and regulatory/legal practitioners advising on admission
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and evaluative criteria used by the USPTO (OED/Director) to decide petitions for reciprocal recognition of foreign attorneys to represent parties in trademark matters, focusing on good moral character, compliance with regulations and TMEP, and authorized practice rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocal recognition under 37 C.F.R. §10.14(c)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any foreign attorney or agent not a resident of the United States who shall prove to the satisfaction of the Director that he or she is registered or in good standing before the patent or trademark office of the country in which he or she resides and practices, may be recognized for the limited purpose of representing parties located in such country before the Office in the presentation and prosecution of trademark cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The regulation is discretionary (uses 'may be recognized') and the applicant must make the required demonstrations 'to the satisfaction of the [OED] Director.' The predecessor §10.14(c) was carried forward into successor regulation §11.14. Compliance with the formal prerequisites (registered/in good standing in home office) is necessary but not sufficient for recognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good moral character and reputation (35 U.S.C. §2(b)(2)(D))
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO may require persons seeking recognition to show that they are of good moral character and reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good moral character is broader than merely absence of moral turpitude. The USPTO evaluates conduct such as financial mismanagement, falsehoods, misrepresentations, and other irresponsible conduct as relevant to moral character (citing case law). The applicant bears the burden to demonstrate good moral character to the Director's satisfaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unauthorized practice of law is a relevant adverse factor
rubrics_metrics.description: Engaging in the unauthorized practice of law — including filing and prosecuting trademark applications before the USPTO without proper recognition — is a factor adverse to a finding of good moral character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts and USPTO decisions treat unauthorized practice as serious conduct (e.g., Colorado v. Corbin; In re Singer). Examples include repeated prosecution over many cases/years (here, >50 cases over more than a decade). Repeated unauthorized practice supports denial of recognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truthfulness and candor: absence of false statements
rubrics_metrics.description: False statements or misrepresentations about one's recognition or status before the USPTO weigh against a finding of good moral character and reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific falsehoods (e.g., a statement claiming that reciprocity had been granted when it had not) are cited as evidence of lack of truthfulness. The Office expects the highest degree of candor and good faith from practitioners (Kingsland v. Dorsey).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ignorance of USPTO rules is not an adequate excuse
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant's claim that noncompliance resulted from ignorance of USPTO rules or confusion over website guidance does not excuse unauthorized practice or false statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TMEP provisions and CFR language are construed to make the limitations clear (e.g., TMEP §602.06(c) when read in full). The applicant is ultimately responsible for complying with rules; the Director's discretionary authority and clear regulatory text mean ignorance is not a defense.

rubrics_metrics.name: TMEP §602.06(c) limitations on what unrecognized foreign attorneys may do
rubrics_metrics.description: A foreign attorney or agent not authorized under 37 C.F.R. may transmit and receive correspondence but 'cannot prepare an application, response, or other paper to be filed in the USPTO, sign responses to Office actions, or authorize examiner's amendments and priority actions.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Partial reading of the TMEP is insufficient; the full section expressly prohibits prosecution activities. Alleged reliance on a single sentence permitting transmission/receipt does not permit the filing/prosecution conduct that constitutes unauthorized practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signature and electronic filing requirements (TMEP §605.02)
rubrics_metrics.description: An authorized signatory must personally sign his/her name; another person may not sign on an attorney's behalf and electronic signatures in TEAS must be entered manually by the person identified as the signer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typing another person's electronic signature is not a valid signature; allowing an assistant to submit documents under the applicant's signature when not admitted constitutes unauthorized practice. The rules require personal entry of electronic signatures and personal signing of submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discretionary nature of recognition ('may be recognized')
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory language indicates that recognition is not automatic even if prerequisites are met: the Director has discretion to approve or deny recognition requests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the regulation uses permissive language ('may be recognized'), the Director's exercise of judgment and discretion is central; applicants must satisfy discretionary standards, including character and compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO's duty to protect the public and expectation of high candor
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office must protect the public and requires a high degree of candor and good faith from practitioners, who occupy a position of trust with respect to applicants and the Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citations (e.g., Kingsland v. Dorsey) emphasize the Office's responsibility to guard against practitioners who betray trust; this underpins rigorous assessment of moral character and conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant's burden of proof to demonstrate good moral character
rubrics_metrics.description: The petitioner bears the burden to show he/she is of good moral character and reputation; failure to meet that burden justifies denial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation of moral character involves 'an exercise of delicate judgment' (Schware v. Bd of Bar Examiners). Even if allegations of intent vs. ignorance exist, the factual record (e.g., sustained unauthorized practice and false statements) can warrant denial when the burden is unmet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance and probative value of supporting evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters and other submissions offered in support of good character must be relevant and probative of moral character and reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mass submissions of thank-you notes and unrelated correspondence have little bearing; only directly relevant attestations (e.g., from colleagues or clients speaking to honesty/reputation) are persuasive. In this case, only a small fraction of voluminous letters were relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of demonstrated client harm is not dispositive
rubrics_metrics.description: Lack of proven harm to clients resulting from the applicant's unauthorized practice does not alone justify granting recognition or excuse the conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statutory and regulatory standards empower the Director to deny recognition based on conduct even if clients were not shown to be harmed; public protection and standards of candor remain controlling considerations.
